title: Design a 100M-Player Distributed Leaderboard at 200K Writes/Sec
prompt: Design a real-time distributed leaderboard for 100,000,000 active players sustaining 200,000 score updates/sec and serving getTopK(100) and getPlayerRank(userId) in < 20 ms p99 with deterministic tie-breaking and zero-downtime season resets.

spark.summary: A single Redis ZSET holding 100M players consumes ~14 GB RAM and saturates one CPU core at ~80K ops/s, causing multi-second RDB fork pauses and dropped score updates. Sharding by `userId % 16`, buffering writes through a `userId`-partitioned Kafka WAL, caching a 16-shard Min-Heap Top-100 for 500 ms, and serving tail ranks from a Score-Range Prefix Histogram holds `getTopK(100)` and `getPlayerRank(userId)` under 20 ms p99.
spark.keyTakeaway: When a single sorted set hits its single-core CPU ceiling and stalls on 14 GB memory snapshots, shard players by user ID across 16 instances, serve Top-100 from a 500 ms merged cache, and estimate tail ranks in O(1) from a score-range histogram instead of scanning all shards.
spark.byteSummary:
Putting 100,000,000 players into one Redis Sorted Set (`ZSET`) breaks in three ways: 100M skip-list + hash entries consume ~14 GB RAM, 200,000 `ZADD`s/sec exceed a single Redis thread's ~80-100K ops/sec ceiling, and `BGSAVE` `fork()` page-table copies trigger multi-second latency spikes.

Sharding across `K = 16` Redis instances by `userId % 16` drops per-shard load to **12,500 writes/sec** and **~875 MB RAM**—leaving 6x CPU headroom and sub-10 ms RDB forks. A `userId`-partitioned Kafka log absorbs bursts and pipelines 100 `ZADD`s per network syscall.

For reads: `getTopK(100)` runs a background 16-shard `ZREVRANGE 0 99` scatter-gather every **500 ms**, merges 1,600 entries in a Min-Heap in <0.5 ms, and serves 100K reads/sec from cache. For `getPlayerRank(userId)`, players in the **Top 10,000** get exact ranks from a merged snapshot, while the remaining 99.99M players read an **O(1) Score-Range Prefix Histogram** (<0.1% variance) instead of scanning 16 shards.

learningJourney.title: Why a Single 14 GB Redis ZSET Collapses at 200K Writes/Sec
learningJourney.purpose: Derive the shard count K = 16 directly from Redis single-thread CPU ceilings, skip-list memory overhead, and OS fork() copy-on-write stalls.

explanation.foundation:
Every `ZADD` into a Redis Sorted Set updates two structures in memory: a dict mapping `userId -> score` (~64 bytes) and a probabilistic **skip list** node with 1-32 forward pointers (~76 bytes). At ~140 bytes per player:

$$\text{Total RAM} = 100\times 10^6 \times 140\text{ B} \approx 14\text{ GB}$$

A single Redis process executes commands on **one main thread**. Even with fast NVMe and 10 Gbps NICs, a single Redis instance saturates around ~80,000–100,000 `ZADD`s/sec when skip-list depth is $\log_2(10^8) \approx 27$ levels. At 200,000 writes/sec, commands queue up, p99 latency explodes past seconds, and `OOM` or dropped connections follow.
explanation.core:
Even if Redis were multi-threaded, a 14 GB single-instance heap breaks on persistence and failover. When `BGSAVE` or `AOF rewrite` calls `fork()`, the Linux kernel copies the parent process's page table (~28 MB for 14 GB at 4 KB pages, or worse under Transparent Huge Pages). During 200K writes/sec, copy-on-write page faults duplicate dirty 4 KB/2 MB pages rapidly, doubling RAM usage and stalling the event loop.

Sizing for **50% safety margin** (target $\le 15\text{K writes/sec}$ and $\le 1.5\text{ GB}$ per shard) yields:

$$K = \max\left(\lceil 200\text{K} / 15\text{K} \rceil, \lceil 14\text{ GB} / 1.5\text{ GB} \rceil\right) = 16\text{ shards}$$

At $K=16$ (`userId % 16`), each shard holds **6.25M players (~875 MB RAM)** and **12,500 writes/sec**.
explanation.deepDive: Why `userId % 16` instead of score-range sharding (e.g., Shard 0 = scores `0..1000`, Shard 1 = `1001..2000`)? Score-range sharding creates severe **write hotspots** (90% of new players sit in the `0..1000` bucket) and forces expensive **cross-shard moves** (`ZREM` on Shard 0 + `ZADD` on Shard 1) whenever a player levels up. Hash sharding by `userId % 16` keeps every player's updates pinned to one shard and balances write load evenly—at the cost of an `O(K)` scatter-gather for global Top-K, which we amortize in Stage 3.

comparison.benefits: O(log N) exact ZREVRANK in 1 call; zero scatter-gather.
comparison.costs: Saturates 1 CPU core at ~90K ZADD/s; multi-second fork() stalls; 14 GB blast radius.

comparison.benefits: Top-K reads hit only the highest score shard.
comparison.costs: Massive write skew on beginner score ranges; non-atomic cross-shard moves on score jumps.

comparison.benefits: Uniform 12.5K ZADD/s & ~875 MB/shard; single-shard atomic ZADD.
comparison.costs: Global Top-K requires merging K=16 shards (solved via 500 ms cache).

learningJourney.title: Surviving Bursts: Kafka Partitioned WAL & Pipelined ZADD
learningJourney.purpose: Explain why direct synchronous API-to-Redis writes drop updates during failovers and how userId-partitioned Kafka + pipelining protects ordering.

explanation.foundation: If the Score API calls Redis `ZADD` synchronously inside the HTTP handler, two things break under load: (1) 200,000 individual TCP round-trips/sec burn huge kernel `epoll`/syscall overhead; (2) a 3-second Redis primary failover drops or times out 600,000 score updates.
explanation.core:
Instead, `POST /v1/scores` validates the payload, publishes an event `(userId, absoluteScore, ts, matchId)` to a **Kafka topic partitioned by `userId`** (32+ partitions), and returns `202 Accepted` in <3 ms. Partitioning by `userId` guarantees all updates for a given player arrive in strict causal order.

Consumer workers pull batches of 100–250 events and flush them to each Redis shard using **Redis pipelining**—cutting network round-trips by 100x while keeping per-batch latency under 5 ms.
explanation.deepDive: Always send **absolute scores** (`ZADD key score userId`) rather than relative increments (`ZINCRBY key delta userId`) whenever possible. If a Kafka consumer crashes after flushing a pipeline to Redis but before committing its Kafka offset, replaying `ZINCRBY +50` double-credits the player, whereas `ZADD 1450` (guarded by `ZADD GT`—Greater Than—if scores are monotonic) is 100% idempotent.

sectionDiagram.title: Why Kafka WAL + Pipelined Idempotent ZADD Survives Failovers
sectionDiagram.summary: Partitioning Kafka by userId preserves per-player order while pipelined ZADD GT makes consumer replays idempotent.

decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When a single sorted set hits its single-core CPU ceiling and stalls on 14 GB memory snapshots, shard players by user ID across 16 instances, serve Top-100 from a 500 ms merged cache, and estimate tail ranks in O(1) from a score-range histogram instead of scanning all shards.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Scatter-Gather Top-100 via Min-Heap + 500 ms Singleflight Cache
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent 100K read RPS from hitting all 16 Redis shards by merging Top-100 in a K-way Min-Heap behind a 500 ms cache.

explanation.foundation: If 100,000 players open the leaderboard tab simultaneously and each request fans out `ZREVRANGE 0 99` to all 16 shards, Redis receives 1.6M range queries/sec and melts down.
explanation.core: Instead, a **single background refresher** (or `Singleflight`-guarded cache-aside) queries `ZREVRANGE lb:shard_i 0 99 WITHSCORES` across the 16 shards once every **500 ms** (~50 KB total payload). A **size-100 Min-Heap** merges the 1,600 candidates in $O(16 \times 100 \log 100) \approx 10,000$ operations (<0.3 ms) and writes the serialized Top-100 JSON to a read cache/CDN.

sectionDiagram.title: 100K RPS Served from 500 ms Cache via Background Min-Heap Merge
sectionDiagram.summary: Decoupling 100K RPS client reads from a 500 ms background Min-Heap merge caps shard read overhead at 2 QPS/shard.

learningJourney.title: Exact Top-10K Snapshot vs. O(1) Score-Range Histogram for 99.99M Players
learningJourney.purpose: Explain why global ZREVRANK cannot work across 16 shards and how a tiered Top-10K + Score Histogram serves all 100M players in O(1).

explanation.foundation: On a single Redis ZSET, `ZREVRANK` computes exact rank in $O(\log N)$. Across 16 shards, your local rank on Shard 3 tells you nothing about how many players on Shards 0–2 and 4–15 have a higher score—computing exact global rank for player #45,120,000 would require running `ZCOUNT shard_i (score, +inf)` on **all 16 shards** on every profile view!
explanation.core:
Notice the product asymmetry: players in the **Top 10,000** care deeply about exact `#42 vs #43`, while player `#45,120,000` only needs an accurate percentile/bracket (`~#45.1M`).

- **Tier 1 (Top 10,000)**: Background refresher merges `ZREVRANGE 0 9999` across 16 shards every 2s into a fast lookup hash map (`O(1)` exact rank).
- **Tier 2 (Remaining 99.99M)**: Maintain a **Score-Range Prefix Histogram** (e.g., 10,000 fixed/log-width score buckets) updated asynchronously by Kafka consumers (`HINCRBY bucket_new +1`, `HINCRBY bucket_old -1`). Global rank = `sum(buckets > my_bucket) + linear_interp` in **O(1)**!
explanation.deepDive: Even better: because the Kafka consumer already reads the player's old score (or caches it in a compact RocksDB/Redis lookup) before issuing `ZADD`, updating the two histogram bucket counters adds negligible overhead and keeps rank variance under **0.1%**.

learningJourney.title: 53-Bit IEEE-754 Composite Tie-Breaking & Server-Signed Score Guards
learningJourney.purpose: Pack score + inverted timestamp cleanly inside Redis float64's 53-bit exact integer mantissa without silent rounding corruption.

explanation.foundation: Redis stores ZSET scores as **IEEE-754 64-bit floating-point (`double`)**, which only represents integers **exactly** up to $2^{53} - 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991$. Packing a 40-bit score + 32-bit timestamp (72 bits) silently drops low-order bits and breaks tie-breaking!
explanation.core:
Fit the composite score strictly within **53 bits**:

$$\text{composite} = (\text{score} \ll 20) \mid ((\text{MAX\_TS} - \text{ts}) \;\&\; \text{0xFFFFF})$$

This gives **33 bits for score** (up to $8.58 \times 10^9$) and **20 bits for inverted relative timestamp** (~12 days at 1-second resolution, or ~17 minutes at 1-ms resolution within a match). Earlier achievers get a larger inverted timestamp and rank higher on ties!
explanation.deepDive: On the security boundary, never accept raw client scores (`POST /score = 999999999`). Require server-signed match receipts (HMAC/JWT from authoritative game servers), enforce per-minute score-delta anomaly caps, and quarantine cheaters via `ZREM` on their single `userId % 16` shard.

caveats: Never exceed 2^53 - 1 (9.007e15) in Redis ZSET composite scores, or IEEE-754 rounding will corrupt tie-breaker bits.
Never trust client-submitted absolute scores without server-signed match telemetry or delta-velocity checks.

sectionDiagram.title: Packing Score + Inverted Timestamp Inside IEEE-754 Exact Mantissa
sectionDiagram.summary: Keeping composite scores within 53 bits preserves exact tie-breaking without floating-point rounding.

learningJourney.title: Versioned Season Cutovers & Non-Blocking Redis UNLINK
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent multi-second midnight Redis freezes during season resets by switching versioned keys and freeing old ZSETs asynchronously.

explanation.foundation: Calling Redis `DEL lb:shard_0` on a 6.25M-entry ZSET frees 6.25 million heap nodes **synchronously on the single main thread**—freezing the entire Redis shard for 2–4 seconds right at midnight UTC!
explanation.core: Namespace every ZSET by season ID (`lb:s42:shard_0..15`, `lb:s43:shard_0..15`). Pre-warm empty `s43` keys and histogram buckets 5 minutes before midnight. At `00:00:00 UTC`, flip the active season pointer atomically in config/API.
explanation.deepDive: Archive `s42` Top-K and final ranks to S3/Iceberg from a read replica (never the write primary), then reclaim `s42` RAM using `UNLINK lb:s42:shard_i`—which detaches the key in $O(1)$ and frees memory on a background lazy-free thread.

sectionDiagram.title: Zero-Downtime Season Switch with Async UNLINK Reclamation
sectionDiagram.summary: Versioned season namespaces and background UNLINK eliminate midnight reset stalls.

learningJourney.title: 10 ms Shard Timeouts, Replica Isolation & Stale-While-Revalidate
learningJourney.purpose: Keep Top-100 p99 under 20 ms even when a Redis shard fails over or a consumer lags.

explanation.foundation: In a 16-shard scatter-gather, tail latency is governed by the **slowest** of the 16 shards. If Shard 7 stalls for 3 seconds during a Sentinel/Cluster primary promotion, synchronous retries would stall 100% of Top-100 refreshes.
explanation.core: Route read-heavy `ZREVRANGE` refreshes to per-shard **read replicas**, enforce a strict **10 ms per-shard timeout**, and on any shard timeout serve the last good cached Top-100 (`Stale-While-Revalidate`) while incrementing `leaderboard_stale_serve_total`.
explanation.deepDive: On the write side, Kafka retains 24+ hours of score events; once Shard 7's standby promotes to primary (~2-5s), the Kafka consumer automatically replays the missed `ZADD GT` batch with zero data loss.

reflectionQuestions: Why does a 10 ms per-shard timeout + Stale-While-Revalidate outperform synchronous retries on a 16-shard scatter-gather?
How would your histogram update logic handle a player whose score decreases (if penalties exist) vs. monotonically increasing scores?

sectionDiagram.title: Replica Reads + 10 ms Timeout + SWR Fallback During Shard 7 Failover
sectionDiagram.summary: Per-shard 10 ms timeouts and SWR caching shield readers while Kafka replays missed writes onto promoted replicas.

options.text: It reduces total RAM to 1 MB.

options.text: It drops per-shard write rate to 12.5k ZADD/sec and per-shard RAM to ~875 MB, eliminating single-thread saturation and large RDB fork stalls.
options.feedback: Correct: Splitting load 16 ways keeps every Redis node comfortably inside CPU and memory headroom.

Incorrect: It silently rounds the significand rather than throwing OOM.
